primitives.name: Player Efficiency Rating
primitives.verbatim_quote: In basketball, Dean Oliver and John Hollinger were early innovators who argued for evaluating players on a per-minute basis rather than a per-game basis and developed measures of overall player value, like Hollinger's Player Efficiency Rating (PER) (Oliver, 2004, Hollinger, 2005a,b).
primitives.assumptions: Linear additive contribution of individual actions to overall efficiency; constant weighting across metrics.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When player minutes are low or when key metrics are missing (e.g., no blocks or steals recorded).

layer2.mapping: Maps raw box-score counts to scalar efficiency index via weighted linear combination; used in GSI for player ranking and comparative analysis.
layer2.telemetry: Observed player box score statistics over a game period.

The foundational operators—PER, shot modeling, and APM—are derived from core basketball data types: box scores, tracking coordinates, and play-by-play logs. PER synthesizes discrete event counts into a scalar metric, assuming additive contributions. Shot modeling uses logistic regression to predict success probability based on spatial and contextual features, enabling simulation of optimal shot selection. APM estimates player influence via conditional expectation differences, requiring careful control for confounding variables like lineup composition. Each operator exhibits distinct failure modes: PER lacks context sensitivity, shot models depend on feature completeness, and APM suffers from multicollinearity and small-sample instability. These primitives form a dual framework where descriptive metrics (PER, APM) support static evaluation, while predictive models (shot modeling) enable dynamic tactical inference. The interplay between these layers reveals a hierarchy of abstraction: from raw observables to latent performance indicators, then to strategic outcomes.
